title: Patacara's grief
hookLine: Patacara loses her whole family in a day, runs mad with grief, and later becomes a respected teacher (Therigatha commentary)
last: LIKE A WHEEL OR A SHADOW.

lines: A RICH GIRL AND A SERVANT.
cards: A daughter of a wealthy family in the city of Savatthi falls in love with a servant in her parents' house. Her family will never allow it, so the two slip away and make a life somewhere poor and far off.

In time, a child is born. Expecting a second, she wants to go home to her mother to give birth, so with her husband and little boy she sets out for Savatthi. Her name is Patacara, and on this road she loses everything.

teach.h: ONE ROAD, ONE STORM, ONE RIVER.
teach.b: First, one road, one storm, one river. The story is told in the old commentary on the poems of the early Buddhist nuns. On the road a great storm breaks, and her labor begins.
Her husband goes to cut branches for a shelter; a snake bites him, and he dies in the brush. She gives birth in the rain. In the morning a river is in flood.
She carries the newborn across and lays him on the bank. Halfway back for her older boy, a hawk swoops down on the baby.
She screams and waves her arms, and her older son, thinking she's calling him, steps into the river and is swept away.
In the city she learns that in the night her parents' house fell in the storm, and her parents and brother are being burned on a single pyre.
Second, come back to yourself. The story says she lost her mind. Her clothes fell from her; she wandered the streets, and people threw rubbish and drove her off.
She came to the grove where the Buddha was teaching, and he said to her, in effect: sister, recover your mindfulness. And she did. Someone threw her a cloak.
Third, her own poem. Patacara became a nun, and verses under her name survive in the Therigatha itself.

teach.h: HER OWN POEM: WATER ON THE FEET.
teach.b: In them she washes her feet, watches the water run down the slope, and her mind gathers, the way a good horse is trained.
The Anguttara Nikaya names her foremost among the nuns who knew the discipline, the rules of the order. Her poem ends with a lamp, and tomorrow we'll get to it.

how: Buddhists tell Patacara's story from the commentaries and read her verses in the Therigatha, the poems of the early nuns.

o: a mourning rite nuns keep for a full year after a loss
a lament the Buddha composed after his mother's early death
a nun's story of loss, coming back to herself, and teaching

s: Patacara's verses survive in the Therigatha
her own poem, with the water on her feet and a lamp.
the Buddha gave Patacara a long sermon on grief first
the story has him tell her, in effect, to recover her mindfulness.
Patacara stayed on the edges of the order
the Anguttara Nikaya names her foremost among nuns who knew the discipline.

games.q: you're Patacara, on the near bank of a flooded river, with a newborn and a small boy. what do you do?
o: wait for the water to fall
carry the newborn across first, then come back for the older boy
try to carry both at once
games.why: she carried the baby across and turned back for her son; halfway, a hawk came down on the baby, and her son, thinking she called, stepped into the river.

practice: Bring to mind someone you know, or know of, who survived a great loss: a grandparent who buried a child, a friend after a divorce or a death.
Hold the size of what they carried, and notice that they kept going: they got up, cooked, went to work, maybe even taught others. Honor that quietly, without needing to say anything.

wordCard.voice: Patacara's grief: an early Buddhist nun who lost husband, children, parents and brother, came back to herself, and became a teacher of the discipline. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: Patacara, the nun's name as it appears in the Therigatha.

carryVoice: Your line: she walked on. From the streets to a teacher others came to learn from. Seven hundred five days.
